title: An ICE Agent Fatally Shot an Authorized Worker in Maine. It Was the Second Killing in a Week.
excerpt: The 26-year-old Colombian man had a Social Security number and legal work authorization. His death in Biddeford came days after agents killed a Mexican national in Houston. For immigrant communities — including hundreds of thousands of Indians — the enforcement escalation has turned routine encounters into life-or-death moments.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • A 26-year-old Colombian man was fatally shot by ICE agents in Maine.
  • This incident marks the second ICE killing in less than a week.
  • ICE arrests in Maine have quadrupled since June, creating fear among immigrants.
  • Both victims were legally authorized to work in the U.S. at the time of their deaths.
  • Protests erupted in Biddeford, demanding accountability and changes in ICE operations.
Escalating ICE Violence
June 2023
ICE arrests in Maine begin to surge.
July 3, 2023
ICE agents fatally shoot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston.
July 10, 2023
ICE agents fatally shoot a Colombian man in Biddeford, Maine.
A person was fatally shot during an encounter with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Biddeford, Maine, on Monday morning — the second killing by ICE agents in less than a week. Immigration advocates identified the victim as a 26-year-old Colombian man who was authorized to work in the United States and held a Social Security number. The Maine Immigrants' Rights Coalition and Presente! Maine called his death "devastating, enraging, and unacceptable." "His loved ones deserve answers, and the public deserves a full and transparent account of what happened," the groups said in a joint statement. ## What Witnesses Saw Daniel Boucher, a 71-year-old resident of downtown Biddeford, told Reuters he was in his second-floor apartment when he heard what sounded like firecrackers around 7:30 a.m. He ran to the window and saw a white SUV ram a smaller white car more than once, causing the car to change direction. An ICE officer then got out of the SUV and tried to open the other car's door before pulling a man out, Boucher said. The young man had blood on his face and head. The officer placed him on the ground. "Initially I remember hearing the victim say, 'But I tried to stop,'" Boucher recounted. > **""Initially I remember hearing the victim say, 'But I tried to stop,'" Boucher recounted."** The officer who appeared to have fired the shot looked "very distraught, almost in shock," according to Boucher. Videos verified by Reuters showed the white car driving in what appeared to be a confused circle, with two agents in vests on foot trying to stop it. Photos showed the car with what appeared to be bullet holes in the windshield. U.S. Senator Angus King of Maine said he had spoken with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and confirmed the victim was a man in his 20s. King also noted that the agents were apparently not wearing body cameras. ## A Pattern in Six Days The Biddeford killing came just six days after an ICE agent fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during a traffic stop in Houston's heavily Hispanic East End. ICE said Salgado, a Mexican national who had lived in the United States for more than three decades, rammed a law enforcement vehicle and attempted to run over an officer. But the agency has not produced evidence to support that account. Three witnesses have challenged ICE's version of events, according to a lawyer representing two of them. Salgado was a father of three and a construction worker who was in the process of obtaining a work permit, his family said. In both cases, the victims were stopped in their vehicles during routine enforcement operations — not during raids on criminal targets. ## Protests in a Small City About 200 demonstrators gathered at a park in Biddeford, a city of 21,000 people roughly 15 miles south of Portland, before marching to the local office of Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is running for reelection this year. Ten protesters entered the building's foyer, chanting "ICE out!" and "Vote her out!" Democratic Representative Chellie Pingree, who represents the area in Congress, posted a video in which she said she was "deeply disturbed and angry."
Impact on Immigrant Communities
›ICE arrests in Maine increased to around 70 per day.
›Indian Americans are the second-largest immigrant group in the U.S.
›Hundreds of thousands of Indians hold work authorizations.
›Both shooting victims were legally authorized to work.
"More than anything else, I want to know: why are you in Maine?" she said. ## The Enforcement Surge Since the beginning of June, ICE arrests in Maine have more than quadrupled to around 70 per day in early July, according to internal ICE data shared with Reuters. The surge is part of President Donald Trump's nationwide immigration crackdown, which has drawn protests in multiple cities and legal challenges from Democratic-led states. The escalation is not limited to undocumented immigrants. Advocates and attorneys have warned that the aggressive posture of enforcement operations — including vehicle pursuits and the use of lethal force — is creating a climate of fear that extends to all immigrant communities, including those with legal status. ## Why the Diaspora Should Pay Attention Indian Americans are the second-largest immigrant group in the United States, with more than 4.8 million people of Indian origin. Hundreds of thousands hold work authorizations through H-1B visas, H-4 EADs, OPT, or green card applications in process. The fear of encounters with immigration enforcement is not limited to those without documentation. The two ICE killings in a single week — both involving men who were in or seeking legal status — underscore a broader concern: that the current enforcement environment treats every immigrant encounter as a potential confrontation, regardless of the person's legal standing. Civil liberties organizations including the ACLU have called for independent investigations into both shootings and for mandatory body camera use during all ICE enforcement operations. For Indian families navigating the immigration system — waiting for green cards, renewing work permits, or simply driving to work — the question of what happens during an unexpected encounter with federal agents has taken on new urgency. Sources: Reuters, Maine Immigrants' Rights Coalition, Presente! Maine, ACLU
